newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices soar, supply concerns rekindled.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices soar, supply concerns rekindled.

text.p: Coffee prices rose sharply on Wednesday on rekindled concerns about a shortage of supplies for nearby delivery.
At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange the run-up was led by the contract for September delivery, which has rocketed 22.8 cents a pound, or more than 14 percent, in the last two sessions.
"They are worried about September deliveries," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast. "Near-term supply concerns are starting to re-emerge.

"There are very low arabica stocks of Colombian milds and other milds, and that's where the shortage is as far as the New York exchange is concerned," she added. "There is a fear CSCE stocks will go down and that has a certain psychological impact."
September closed at 181.65 cents a pound, up 12.55 cents on the day.

With little certifiable coffee expected to make its way to the exchange ahead of the autumn harvest of new-crop Latin American coffees, many market participants said a drawdown of certified stocks going into the September delivery period was inevitable.

"Stocks should be getting tighter and everyone knows it," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "Stocks have been building up on a steady basis, but by and large producers have finished shipping coffee.
"There should not be much new-crop coffee until about November," he added. "As a result, we should see stocks of arabica coffee tighten up."
However, CSCE reported after Wednesday's close that certified coffee inventories rose by 3,666 60-kg bags as of July 22, to 90,897 bags.
An additional 5,609 bags were pending grading, the exchange said.

Gold prices slipped lower on talk of European central bank selling and on news South Africa's Western Areas Gold Mining Co Ltd said it had completed a buy-back of 1.6 million ounces of a 7.3 million ounce forward sale arranged in 1995.
At the New York Commodity Exchange, gold for August delivery ended down $2.20 at $323.80 an ounce.
Comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan late Tuesday also helped push the U.S. dollar and stock and bond markets sharply higher, pressuring gold prices lower Wednesday.

Greenspan said U.S. economic growth was slowing, inflation in 1997 was modest, and the falling gold price reflected a lowering of inflation expectations, all of which meant a near-term monetary policy tightening could be avoided.
"We view all four precious metals with negative bias," Merrill Lynch senior analyst Bill O'Neill said. "Our $300 downside objective for gold is probably conservative."
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline led oil prices higher on inventory data showing declining supplies.
August gasoline settled 1.10 cents a gallon higher at 61.12 cents. August heating oil ended 0.58 cent up a 53.28 cents a gallon and September crude finished with a 15 cent gain at $19.63 a barrel.

Gasoline was boosted by data issued by the U.S. Department of Energy on Wednesday that showed for the week ended July 18, gasoline stocks fell by 2.3 million barrels, a steeper decline than traders had expected.
Stocks issued by the private American Petroleum Institute for the same week had also indicated a substantial drawdown of 2.8 million barrels.
The DOE and the API report inventory data weekly, although oil companies are obligated to report stock data to the DOE while they voluntarily report to the API, an oil industry trade group.
Reports from U.N. headquarters in New York indicated an aid distribution plan, which Iraq says must be finalised before exports can resume, will not be approved before the weekend.
Traders expected that agreeing new price formulas and signing new contracts will take a further two weeks, suggesting an earliest start date for sales of mid-August.
